lesson.title: The H–R diagram

steps.headline: A star's luminosity grows with its surface area and, much faster, with its temperature.

lead.text: Each square metre of surface emits power proportional to T⁴, and the surface area is 4πR². In solar units, with R in solar radii and T measured against the Sun's 5,772 K, this becomes L = R²(T/T☉)⁴.

steps.headline: Find the luminosity of a star with R = 2 R☉ and T = 1.5 T☉.

workedSteps.text: Write the law in solar units.

lead.text: The radius stays at the Sun's, so R² = 1. Only the temperature changes.

reveal.text: Doubling the temperature multiplies the luminosity by 2⁴, so temperature is a far stronger lever than radius.

steps.headline: The H–R diagram plots luminosity against temperature, and stars fall into groups.

lead.text: Temperature runs backwards, with the hottest stars on the left. Most stars lie on the main sequence, a diagonal band. Up and to the right sit cool stars so luminous they must be enormous: giants and supergiants. Down on the left are hot, dim white dwarfs.
Up and to the right sit cool stars so luminous they must be enormous. Work out how luminous one is.

reveal.text: A cool surface alone would make the star dim. Only an enormous radius gives it tens of thousands of times the Sun's output.

lead.text: Down in the lower left lie white dwarfs: hot but dim, so they must be tiny. Lines of constant radius slant across the diagram.

reveal.text: A star the size of Earth, yet hotter than the Sun, gives out only a few hundredths of the Sun's power.

lead.text: On the diagram, stars of equal temperature sit in a vertical line. Moving up that line raises the luminosity but not the power per square metre.

reveal.text: Equal temperature means equal power per square metre, so extra luminosity has to come from extra surface area. Height on the diagram at fixed temperature measures size.

lesson.orientation: Relate luminosity, radius and temperature, and read a star's size from its place on the diagram.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Two stars have the same surface temperature, so each square metre of surface shines equally. Star A has twice the radius of star B.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find a star's luminosity from its radius and temperature, and read its type from the H–R diagram.

recap.keyIdea: A star's luminosity is L = R²(T/T☉)⁴: temperature matters most, then radius. On the H–R diagram that sorts stars into the main sequence, giants and white dwarfs.

blocks.text: You found that doubling the radius quadruples the light at the same temperature, that doubling the temperature multiplies it by 16, and that a cool supergiant gives about 87,000 L☉.

recap.nextHook: A star's place on the diagram depends on its mass. How does mass set how long a star lives?

questions.prompt: A star has the Sun's radius but twice the Sun's surface temperature. How many times the Sun's luminosity does it emit?
hints: Use L = R²(T/T☉)⁴ in solar units.
The radius factor is one.
Raise the temperature ratio to the fourth power.
questions.onCorrect: 16. Luminosity goes as T⁴, so doubling the temperature multiplies it by 2⁴.

misconceptions.feedback: That treats luminosity as proportional to T². It follows the fourth power.
That doubles the luminosity with the temperature. Each square metre emits power proportional to T⁴.
That is 2³. The power per square metre goes as T⁴.

questions.prompt: A red supergiant has a surface temperature of 3,600 K and a radius of 760 R☉. With T☉ = 5,772 K, find its luminosity in solar units, to the nearest thousand.
hints: Square the radius in solar radii.
Raise 3,600/5,772 to the fourth power.
Multiply the two results, then round.
questions.onCorrect: 87,000 L☉. The huge R² outweighs the cool surface's small T⁴ factor.

misconceptions.feedback: That is R² alone. Multiply it by the temperature factor (T/T☉)⁴ as well.
That is the temperature factor alone. Multiply it by R² too.

questions.prompt: A white dwarf has radius 0.01 R☉ and a surface temperature four times the Sun's. Find its luminosity in solar units, to four decimal places.
hints: Square the radius.
Raise the temperature factor to the fourth power.
Multiply 0.0001 by 256.
questions.onCorrect: 0.0256 L☉. A tiny R² beats a hot T⁴: hot but dim.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the radius factor alone. Multiply by the temperature factor as well.
That is the temperature factor alone. Multiply by R² as well.

questions.prompt: Two stars have the same surface temperature, but one is far more luminous. Which property of the luminous star must be larger? Answer in one word.
hints: Write L = 4πR²σT⁴ and hold T fixed.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Its radius. Equal temperature means equal power per square metre, so more luminosity needs more surface area.

questions.onCorrect: Radius: equal temperature means equal power per square metre, so more luminosity needs more surface.

misconceptions.feedback: Both stars share the same temperature, so temperature is not what differs. Think about the surface area.

questions.prompt: Two stars have equal temperatures; one is 100 times as luminous as the other. How many times larger is its radius?
hints: Hold T constant in L ∝ R²T⁴.
Luminosity then scales as radius squared.
Take the square root of the luminosity ratio.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: With T fixed, L ∝ R², so R grows as √100 = 10.

questions.onCorrect: 10 times. At fixed T, L ∝ R², so the radius grows as the square root of L.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the luminosity ratio. L goes as R², so the radius ratio is its square root.
That squares the ratio. The radius ratio is the square root of the luminosity ratio.

questions.prompt: A star twice the Sun's radius has a luminosity of 4 L☉. Taking T☉ = 5,772 K, find its surface temperature in kelvin.
hints: Write L = R²(T/T☉)⁴ and substitute R = 2.
Divide both sides by R².
Find what temperature ratio raised to the fourth power gives the result.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 4 = 2² × (T/T☉)⁴ gives (T/T☉)⁴ = 1, so T equals the Sun's temperature: 5,772 K.

questions.onCorrect: 5,772 K. Divide L by R² first, then take the fourth root of what is left.

misconceptions.feedback: That scales the temperature with the radius. L depends on R² and on T⁴, so divide out R² first.
That halves the temperature. Divide L by R² first, then take the fourth root.

questions.prompt: How many times more light does star A give out in total?
hints: Total light is the light per square metre times the surface area.
Area grows with the square of the radius.
Square the 2.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each square metre shines equally, and surface area goes as radius squared: 2² = 4 times.

questions.onCorrect: 4 times. At equal temperature, luminosity follows the surface area, which goes as R².

misconceptions.feedback: Doubling the radius doubles the width, but a surface has two dimensions.
That uses volume. Light leaves through the surface, not through the volume.

questions.prompt: A star has the Sun's radius and the Sun's temperature. What is its luminosity in solar units?
hints: Put R = 1 and T = T☉ into the formula.
questions.onCorrect: With R = 1 and T = T☉ both factors are 1, so L = 1 L☉: the Sun itself.

misconceptions.feedback: Both factors are 1 here. Nothing multiplies the result by four.
The Sun shines, and a star identical to it must do the same.

questions.prompt: Why does temperature count for more than radius?
hints: Compare the exponents in L = R²(T/T☉)⁴.

acceptedIdeas: T is raised to the fourth power and R only to the second.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: T is raised to the fourth power and R only to the second.

choices.label: T is raised to the fourth power and R only to the second.
The Sun's temperature is the largest.

questions.onCorrect: A fourth power grows faster than a square, so a change in T moves L more than the same change in R.

misconceptions.feedback: Hot stars are not necessarily bigger. The reason is in the exponents.
Many stars are hotter than the Sun. The reason is in the exponents.

questions.prompt: Where on the H–R diagram are the hottest stars?
hints: Temperature runs backwards on this diagram.
questions.onCorrect: The temperature axis runs backwards, so the hottest stars are on the left.

misconceptions.feedback: Cool stars are on the right, because the temperature axis runs backwards.
Height shows luminosity, not temperature. Look along the horizontal axis.

questions.prompt: A star has half the Sun's radius and twice the Sun's surface temperature. Find its luminosity in solar units.
hints: Use L = R²(T/T☉)⁴ with R = 0.5 and T/T☉ = 2.
Work out each factor separately.
Multiply the radius factor by the temperature factor.
questions.onCorrect: 4 L☉. A small radius costs a factor of 0.25 and the hotter surface gains a factor of 16.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the radius factor alone. The hotter surface multiplies it as well.
That is the temperature factor alone. The smaller radius divides it.
